No—I did not fix repository code. I only reproduced the problem in `/tmp`.

The ideal user path should be:

```bash
lobu login
lobu org set <slug>
lobu apply
lobu run
```

After a successful Cloud `lobu apply`, the CLI should automatically persist the project’s Cloud context/org. Then `lobu run` can mint a Cloud-backed Slack code even though it also starts a local runtime.

Today, the reliable workaround is explicit:

```bash
lobu context use lobu
lobu login
lobu org set <slug>
lobu link --org <slug>   # writes .lobu/project.json
lobu apply
lobu run
```

Then, inside Lobu’s Slack:

```text
/lobu link <code>
```

Important distinctions:

- `lobu apply` runs on your local computer but deploys the configuration to Lobu Cloud.
- CLI `lobu link --org …` only pins the local project directory to its Cloud context/org.
- Slack `/lobu link <code>` is sent inside Slack; it binds that Slack DM/channel to the Cloud agent.
- A hosted Slack claim cannot currently bind the hosted Cloud bot directly to the sandbox’s local runtime. Supporting that would require a Cloud-to-local relay/tunnel.
- Purely local `lobu apply -c local` works for the local UI/API, but not for Lobu’s hosted Slack bot.

The code fix I recommend is:

1. After successful Cloud `lobu apply`, automatically save `.lobu/project.json`.
2. Make hosted-preview generation reject the `local` context instead of displaying the misleading “run apply” message.
3. Update the landing prompt to distinguish project-owner Cloud login from customer Slack participation.
4. Add an E2E regression test covering first and second `lobu run`.

Customers still need no Lobu login or workspace installation; they only join Lobu’s Slack. The builder performs the one-time Cloud setup.

Yes, keep CLI `lobu link`, but remove it from the normal happy path.

Ideal behavior:

- Successful Cloud `lobu apply` automatically saves the project link.
- `lobu link` remains an explicit recovery/retargeting command for switching orgs or contexts.
- Consider renaming it to `lobu project link` eventually, because it is easily confused with Slack `/lobu link`.

Login requirements:

- CLI `lobu link --org <slug>`: does **not** currently require Lobu login. It only writes `.lobu/project.json`. It needs a known context and org slug, but does not validate membership.
- Creating the hosted Slack code: **does require the project owner to be logged into Lobu**, because the Cloud claim endpoint requires an authenticated organization user.
- Slack `/lobu link <code>`: does **not** require the Slack participant to log into Lobu. They only need to be signed into Slack and present in the relevant workspace.

So the desired customer path is simply:

```text
Join Lobu’s Slack → send /lobu link <code> → talk to the agent
```

The builder handles `lobu login` and `lobu apply` beforehand.

content.text:
No—this was not just a prompt problem. I found and fixed a real production Slack configuration failure, then completed the hosted `/lobu link` E2E.

What worked:

- Latest CLI created a hosted Slack claim.
- `lobu link --context lobu --org buremba` worked locally.
- `/lobu link <code>` linked the test channel to `personal-agent`.
- A real `@Lobu` message routed to that agent and returned `LINK_OK`.
- Slack participants did not need a Lobu login.

What was broken:

- The production Slack app’s `/lobu` command still targeted the removed `/lobu/slack/events` endpoint, producing “app did not respond.”
- I changed it to `/lobu/api/v1/app-webhooks/slack`.
- I also corrected Slack’s outdated command hint from `connect | login | help` to `link <code> | try <agent-id> | help`.

The onboarding gap is that we currently combine two different questions:

1. How should administrators manage/deploy the agent?
2. Where should users talk to it?

The prompt only asks the second one in [chrome.tsx](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu-ai/landing/src/components/landing/chrome.tsx:17), and then silently prefers hosted Slack. It should explicitly offer:

| Path | Who authenticates | User experience |
|---|---|---|
| Lobu hosted Slack | Builder logs into Lobu once; users only need Slack | Join `https://lobu.ai/slack`, DM `@Lobu`, run `/lobu link <code>` |
| Customer’s Slack | Workspace admin approves Slack OAuth | Install from `https://app.lobu.ai/lobu/slack/install`, link a channel, then mention `@Lobu` |
| Lobu UI | Each user needs Lobu org access | Manage and use agents through `app.lobu.ai` |
| API/MCP | Application/service credentials | Embed the agent in another product or client |

Two more product gaps surfaced:

- In channels, users must mention `@Lobu`; unmentioned messages are not delivered. The current success text says “Say hi,” which is misleading and should say “Mention `@Lobu` in this channel.”
- `lobu run` switches the global context to `local`, then its local auto-apply is rejected because the project is linked to Cloud. That project-link mismatch is a genuine CLI lifecycle bug.
- The Slack documentation is mostly written for operators configuring an app, not customers choosing the hosted workspace, their own Slack, or the Lobu UI.
- The hosted Slack app configuration should be source-controlled or smoke-tested so its endpoints cannot drift again.

We should keep `lobu link`. It records which context and organization a local project targets; it is not a login operation and can write that association without asking for Lobu credentials. Cloud `apply` and hosted claim creation still require the builder to have an authenticated Lobu context.

I made no tracked repository changes yet—the live Slack configuration was fixed externally. The temporary E2E project was removed, the active CLI context is restored to `lobu`, and unrelated untracked workspace files were untouched. The proper implementation should be two focused changes: onboarding/docs copy, followed separately by the `lobu run` local-versus-Cloud lifecycle fix.

I’m using the Lobu operator guidance and the prior onboarding decisions to separate what the agent should demonstrate automatically from what must remain an explicit user choice—especially connector access and managed Slack.

Yes—but encourage a thin, working vertical slice, not a large speculative system based only on the company website.

The ideal onboarding should feel like:

1. Ask at most three questions:

   - What does your company do, and what is its domain?
   - What recurring outcome should this agent handle first?
   - Where should people interact with it: hosted Slack, their Slack workspace, or Lobu UI?

2. Research the public domain, then confirm the understanding with the user. Website research should generate hypotheses, not silently define their data model.

3. Propose a starter blueprint in plain language:

   - “Remember”: 2–4 relevant entity types.
   - “Watch”: one connector/feed.
   - “Do”: one Behavior.
   - “Deliver”: Slack, UI, or both.

For example, a SaaS company might get:

- Entities: customer, account, support issue.
- Source: Slack or GitHub.
- Behavior: daily customer-risk digest.
- Demonstration: ingest one real item, create/update an entity, run the Behavior, and deliver the result to Slack with source provenance.

Users should not be asked, “Which entity types and Behaviors do you want?” The agent should translate their business language into those Lobu concepts and offer a small recommendation for confirmation.

The managed-auth choices should also be explicit:

- Hosted Lobu Slack: join using the invite and paste the generated code. Chat users do not need a Lobu login.
- Customer’s Slack workspace: an admin installs Lobu once; ordinary users can DM or mention the agent without individual Lobu accounts.
- Lobu UI: users log in to Lobu.
- Local developer flow: the operator running `lobu link`/`lobu apply` authenticates to Lobu Cloud; that login should not be confused with customer onboarding.

Most importantly, the completion gate must be an actual useful result:

```text
real input
→ connector/event
→ remembered knowledge or entity
→ Behavior execution
→ visible Slack/UI output
```

Generating config, applying it, or creating a Slack binding is not enough. Our test demonstrated why: the link and Behavior worked, but the isolated agent still could not answer because no model provider was configured. Onboarding should verify provider readiness and require one genuine response before declaring success.

The generated `AGENTS.md` already explains Lobu’s mechanics well. Its main prompt gap is the missing discovery → recommendation → build → demonstrate contract. I would add something like:

```text
Your onboarding objective is a working first outcome, not merely a scaffold.

Ask for the company domain, desired recurring outcome, and preferred interaction
surface. Research public company information, summarize your understanding, and
propose the smallest useful Lobu blueprint: up to four entity types, one source,
and one Behavior.

Explain recommendations in business language before introducing Lobu terminology.
Do not connect private services or apply externally visible configuration without
the user's confirmation. Prefer managed authentication when available.

Finish by demonstrating one real end-to-end path through ingestion, memory,
Behavior execution, and Slack or UI delivery. Do not report success until the
agent produces an actual response and the user can see the resulting data.
```

So: prompt improvement is the first move. Product improvements should then make managed authentication and connector `next_action` steps deterministic enough that the agent can complete that promised demonstration reliably.

Not all of them. In the live `@lobu/cli` 14.11.0 dogfood, `lobu run` printed:

- API docs: `http://localhost:8788/api/docs`
- A tokenized Web UI URL
- The `lobu chat -c local "hello"` command

It did not print these, although I verified they are served:

- REST base: `http://localhost:8788/lobu/api/v1`
- MCP: `http://localhost:8788/lobu/mcp`

So an agent running the command sees the Web UI and docs, but must already know the REST/MCP conventions. In a remote sandbox, it also sees `localhost`, not the externally usable proxy URL.

The ideal fix is for `lobu run` to print a complete “Access” block containing Web UI, API docs, REST, MCP, token command, and—when detectable—the external/proxy URL. A machine-readable `--json` output would make this reliable for coding agents.

The dogfood also uncovered two separate blockers:

- Public GitHub ingestion still requires `GITHUB_TOKEN` at the Lobu platform layer, despite GitHub supporting anonymous public reads.
- No Lobu model provider is configured, so we correctly stopped before claiming a generated answer.

content.text:
Yes. `GITHUB_TOKEN` appeared because our dogfood selected the wrong fallback, not because it is the intended customer path.

What happened:

- The GitHub connector’s preferred method is the managed GitHub App.
- Our initial local config declared a plain GitHub connection without `managedBy`.
- `lobu apply` returned a structured “setup required” response, but the CLI reduced it to the misleading `returned no connection payload`.
- We then explicitly tested the `env` fallback, which correctly requires `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

I corrected the dogfood to:

```ts
managedBy: { org: "lobu-team" }
```

The local connection and feeds were created. But token delegation returned 404 because the existing `lobu-team` GitHub App installation is a private workspace installation, not a user-owned grant that local runtimes may export. That isolation is correct—we must not let customers silently borrow Lobu’s own GitHub installation.

The intended customer journey should be:

1. `lobu login` identifies the customer.
2. Lobu offers “Install our managed GitHub App.”
3. The customer installs it into their GitHub organization/account.
4. Lobu stores the installation in their workspace.
5. Local `lobu run` receives short-lived installation access through managed auth—never the stored private key or durable credentials.
6. `GITHUB_TOKEN` remains an explicit BYO/offline fallback only.

The current gap is that this managed GitHub App journey works in hosted workspaces, but local `lobu run` cannot yet seamlessly delegate a customer’s App installation. Existing local `managedBy` delegation supports user-owned, consent-only public managed OAuth grants—not these workspace GitHub App installations.

Also, neither form of “link” solves GitHub auth:

- `lobu link` only associates the local directory with a Lobu context/org.
- `/lobu link <code>` is hosted Slack/Telegram channel binding.

So: we have the managed App foundation, but the local handoff is incomplete. We should fix that and stop onboarding agents from suggesting `GITHUB_TOKEN` before offering the managed installation flow.

Exactly: no login to discover what Lobu supports; login only when accessing or changing the user’s workspace.

The ideal flow:

1. Agent anonymously discovers supported connectors, capabilities, and authentication options.
2. User chooses Lobu-managed or BYO auth.
3. If Lobu-managed is selected and no session exists:
   - If the agent has a trusted email previously supplied by the user, it can initiate email login.
   - Otherwise it asks for the email.
4. Lobu sends a magic-link email.
5. The user clicks once to sign in/create their account and approve.
6. The agent polls automatically, opens the relevant connector installation, and resumes after completion.

Much of this already exists:

- Connector catalog and SDK documentation have public-read discovery surfaces.
- Workspace-specific connection status intentionally requires identity.
- `lobu login --email <address>` already starts the `user_claimed` flow, emails a one-click link, polls for approval, and creates the account on first use.
- External agents can discover the same HTTP flow through `/auth.md`.

“Autonomously” should mean the user’s intent authorizes it. If they say “use Lobu-managed auth” and the agent knows a verified email, it can send the login email and report:

> I sent a Lobu sign-in link to e***@company.com. Click it and I’ll continue automatically.

It should not send unsolicited login emails merely because it found an address through company research. If the email is uncertain, newly inferred, or there are multiple choices, ask first.

The missing glue is for connector setup to return a structured flow like:

```json
{
  "status": "authentication_required",
  "recommended_auth": "lobu_managed",
  "email_login_supported": true,
  "setup_url": "...",
  "completion_check": "..."
}
```

Then the agent can seamlessly perform discovery → email login → workspace selection → connector installation → E2E demonstration without making the user understand tokens, contexts, or auth profiles.

Yes—you’re right. We already have most of the API. I overstated the missing glue as if we needed a new contract.

Existing pieces:

- Discovery: `manage_catalog(list_catalog|list_installed)` and `search_sdk`.
- Authentication discovery: `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and `/auth.md`.
- Email login: OAuth client registration → device authorization → `/oauth/device/email` → poll `/oauth/token`.
- CLI wrapper: `lobu login --email <address>`.
- Connector setup: `manage_connections(connect)` or `client.connections.connect(...)`.
- Setup continuation: returns `setup_required`, `setup_family`, setup/connect URL, `resume_call`, and `completion_check`.
- GitHub App installation: already represented by the `app_installation` setup flow.
- Completion: agent polls the connection until it becomes active, then creates feeds and demonstrates the result.

So this is primarily an agent/onboarding and CLI orchestration problem:

1. Discover connectors.
2. Ask managed versus BYO.
3. If managed and unauthenticated, initiate the existing email flow.
4. Continue with the existing connector setup response.
5. Poll completion and resume automatically.

The dogfood failed because `lobu apply` treated `setup_required` as “no connection payload,” and OpenCode then chose the `GITHUB_TOKEN` fallback. It should have handed control to the existing interactive `connections.connect` continuation.

The one genuine backend gap remains specifically local reuse of a managed GitHub App installation: `managedBy` currently cannot delegate an ordinary private-workspace App installation such as `lobu-team` to a local runtime. But discovery, email authentication, browser setup, and continuation APIs already exist—we need to teach and wire the onboarding agent to use them correctly.

content.text:
Short answer: agents do not automatically know that managed connector auth lives in `lobu-cloud` yet. That is still an onboarding discovery gap.

Current flow:

1. The generated local connection must contain:

```ts
managedBy: { org: "lobu-cloud" }
```

2. `lobu apply` persists that marker in local connection config ([map-config.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/cli/src/commands/_lib/apply/map-config.ts:804)).

3. At runtime, Lobu reads the marker and calls the cloud token endpoint with:

```json
{ "org": "lobu-cloud", "connector_key": "google.gmail" }
```

([execution-context.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/utils/execution-context.ts:224))

There is one automatic path: exporting a consent-only cloud connection through `init-from-org` generates `managedBy` using that cloud org’s slug ([bootstrap.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/cli/src/commands/_lib/init-from-org/bootstrap.ts:1064)).

What is missing:

- `organizations.list()` exposes `lobu-cloud` only as another public workspace; it has no “canonical managed-auth provider” marker.
- The connector catalog does not advertise `managed_by_org`.
- The onboarding agent prompt explains connector discovery but not Lobu-managed authentication.
- `lobu init`’s “Lobu Cloud” option configures memory only—not managed connectors ([init.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/cli/src/commands/init.ts:539)).

The correct fix is structured discovery, such as returning this with connector availability:

```json
{
  "credential_mode": "managed",
  "managed_by_org": "lobu-cloud",
  "requires_user_consent": true
}
```

Then agents can offer Lobu-managed auth without guessing or hard-coding a prompt.

Yes, after merge and deployment I’ll run a clean SSH-visible E2E that proves:

- a fresh agent discovers `lobu-cloud`;
- the user grant remains consent-only with zero cloud feeds;
- local `lobu apply` generates/persists `managedBy`;
- no local OAuth secret/profile is required;
- Gmail token resolution succeeds through `lobu-cloud`;
- Gmail data is read/synced locally, not copied into the public cloud workspace.

content.text:
Yes—the intended path is:

```text
lobu init → lobu run → build/test locally → lobu apply → hosted agent
```

What today’s clean test proved:

- Local embedded Postgres, Web UI, agent, Behaviors and feeds can run locally.
- Managed Gmail authentication works without customer Google OAuth credentials.
- Local auto-apply completed successfully after correcting the generated Behavior.
- The chat request reached Z.ai through Lobu’s secret proxy, but Z.ai returned HTTP 429, so inference did not finish.
- No Gmail content was read and nothing was deployed to cloud.

Important caveats:

- `lobu apply` deploys declarative configuration—not local data or secret values.
- Managed connectors still require Lobu Cloud/internet; the core runtime can remain local.
- `lobu apply` currently ends with “Apply complete”; it does not clearly print every hosted Web UI, MCP, SDK and channel URL. `lobu run` prints the local Web UI and hosted Slack/link instructions, but the final handoff is fragmented.
- The onboarding agent confused Gmail feed `eventKinds` with supported Behavior triggers. The prompt/docs need to teach capability discovery before generating Behaviors.
- The disposable sandbox expired, so its SSH session is gone.
- Please rotate the `Z_AI_API_KEY`: it appeared in the tmate transcript during the failed initial transfer.

So the architecture supports the experience, but the ideal one-command handoff still needs product work: after `lobu apply`, print a single access summary containing Web UI, agent chat, MCP/SDK, connector setup, Slack/Telegram options, and have the agent explain/share those URLs. No repository fix was merged for that yet.

What worked:

- The agent interviewed you about the agent’s purpose, behavior, users, memory, data source, channel, schedule, and model provider.
- Given `lobu.ai`, it produced a relevant “Lobu Signal Scout” with Company, Person, and Signal entities plus Gmail triage and digest Behaviors.
- Managed Gmail authentication worked without customer-owned Google OAuth credentials.
- Local runtime booted, health returned 200, and local auto-apply created the agent, Behaviors, connection, feed, and Z.ai provider.
- Managed-auth PR #2470 remains merged in `origin/main`, and CLI `14.12.0` remains npm `latest`.

What did not work:

- The current [setup prompt](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu-ai/landing/src/components/landing/chrome.tsx:8) does not ask for:

  - Company/business name
  - Public domain
  - Work email
  - Permission to research the company
  - Existing product, customers, workflows, or business model

- It does not instruct the agent to research the domain and propose tailored entities, connectors, and Behaviors.
- OpenCode initially requested BYO OAuth credentials instead of discovering managed auth.
- It confused Gmail feed event types with supported Behavior triggers.
- It generated an invalid source query using `events.content`.
- We corrected those issues during the session.
- The final real chat reached Z.ai through Lobu’s secret proxy, but Z.ai returned HTTP 429. We never received the expected `READY`.
- The Isorun sandbox then expired. The generated project and SSH session are therefore not intact or recoverable.

So the honest verdict is: the underlying local/runtime/managed-auth path works, but autonomous business discovery → correct project generation → real agent response → cloud deployment was not completed in one clean uninterrupted run.

The onboarding prompt should explicitly add:

1. “What company or product is this for?”
2. “What is its public domain?”
3. “May I research that public website and related public sources?”
4. “Is this email your work identity, or should I use another company identity?”
5. Research the company, then present findings with sources.
6. Propose relevant entities, relationships, connectors, Behaviors, and channels.
7. Wait for confirmation before scaffolding.
8. Discover actual connector capabilities and managed-auth offers—never guess triggers or request BYO credentials first.
9. Prove local chat, connector sync, Behavior, memory output, and UI.
10. Run `lobu apply --dry-run`, confirm the target organization, apply, and return every hosted URL.

That prompt/product correction has not been implemented or merged yet.

So even perfect guidance in the template would never reach the agent on exactly the path we want customers to use. content.text: what changes are you doing, are they slop or real problem?

They are real fixes, but one reviewer suggestion was slop—and I caught and reverted it.

The concrete product problems found in the fresh OpenCode run were:

- `lobu init --from-org` produced a cloud export, not a runnable local project: it lacked generated `AGENTS.md`, `TESTING.md`, a protected `.env`, embedded Postgres settings, encryption key, and safe free ports.
- The copied onboarding prompt conflated Lobu email login with Slack OAuth, invented a Slack feed even though Slack exposes none, did not ask which Slack surfaces or people scope to prove, tried `--force` after an empty membership result, tried reading `.env`, and ran commands from the wrong directory.
- The prompt did not distinguish DM, channel mention, App Home/Slackbot, and member discovery as separate E2E checks.
- The landing CI had no regression test for this copied prompt.

The slop was a Codex reviewer claiming installed connector discovery omitted schemas and required direct SQL. Current source proves `catalog.listInstalled()` already returns those schemas. I rejected that change and restored the direct SDK path.

So the current diff is intentionally limited to:

- making `--from-org` bootable locally;
- making generated agent guidance accurate and E2E-oriented;
- updating the landing copy to match;
- adding regression tests and running them in CI.

It does not alter Slack runtime behavior. And I have not yet claimed the `lobusandbox` DM/channel/App Home/member flow works—that live proof is still outstanding and is the point of the fresh post-release run. I’m cutting off the overlong review archaeology now and moving to the actual ship-and-E2E path.

content.text: I’m continuing from the exact release and E2E state. One correction first: the earlier tmate session died when the large prompt was pasted into the TUI; I rebuilt it with the prompt loaded safely. I’m verifying the replacement SSH endpoint and the live OpenCode pane now, while also checking whether the UI approval landed so I can unblock both merges.

The replacement read-only session is live at:

`ssh ro-2Bw2HZT9vpyaKvxV8kuDT2Tzg@nyc1.tmate.io`

The old SSH endpoints should be discarded. I’m keeping this one as the durable observation session; the shell/OpenCode run remain inside its windows rather than a foreground process tied to my connection.

The release state is clean and narrowly blocked:

- PR #2481: every code check passes; only the required human UI approval is pending.
- PR #2482: every substantive check passes; its drift check will become valid only after #2481 updates the Owletto pointer.
- OpenCode completed the guided interview, proposed the right hosted-vs-existing-Slack and people-scope boundaries, and is now proceeding with research/scaffolding after explicit confirmation.

I’m checking the actual Owletto review thread (the approval belongs there, not on the parent PR) and continuing the live OpenCode run meanwhile.

The human gate has not been approved yet. Please inspect the [seven-panel UI comparison](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://gist.githubusercontent.com/buremba/ba38433361ce9d017220edb840f2b81d/raw/6c3ae8c14523bededf9e71c4799a5a3662e81aeb/lobu-agent-navigation-comparison.html), then—if it looks correct—post this exact comment on [Owletto PR #714](https://github.com/lobu-ai/owletto/pull/714):

`/ui-approve 125ffeae49ca0f173a76141fd1f55f7116d63837`

I can’t honestly make that human visual judgment on your behalf. It is the sole current blocker to merging the pointer PR and then the Slack fix. OpenCode is meanwhile installing the published Lobu CLI (`14.13.0`) and inspecting available contexts in the fresh sandbox.

I just reproduced the “not valid” part against production, and there is a second real bug beyond Slack formatting: the URL returns the gateway’s generic JSON health response instead of a connector claim page. So the raw URL is syntactically fine, but its destination is not wired as a web route.

That means PR #2482 is necessary for tenancy/copy correctness, but it is not yet sufficient for your reported experience. I’m tracing where the canonical claim route should live before changing anything; I’ll keep this fix within the same Slack-onboarding concern if it is a small missing route, otherwise I’ll separate it cleanly.

Correction after testing with a real browser `Accept` header: the web route is deployed and serves the Owletto app; my first probe used curl’s API-style `Accept: */*`, which intentionally hit the gateway JSON fallback. So I’m not going to add a bogus route fix.

The actual failure remains the claim semantics: this particular `ref=E0BDSKL1KJL` is the Enterprise installation reference, and that installation is already owned by the Community organization. The page must explain that ownership conflict clearly and offer the correct path—it must not imply the organization disappeared or emit an opaque “invalid link.” I’m inspecting the current page’s exact branch and tests now.

The fresh-agent behavior is now correct at the auth boundary: it did not assume the email grants access. It discovered no Lobu cloud session, explained that Lobu will email `emrekabakci@gmail.com`, and asked before initiating device login. Since you already explicitly chose that account for this dogfood run, I’m authorizing that login attempt; I’ll surface the exact device link/code if it needs you.

The local worktree does not carry a production database URL, so I’m not going to manufacture an auth session or broaden secret access. I’m using the paired Owletto connection you explicitly authorized instead: it will open the claim link in the already logged-in browser and read only the rendered text, which is the most faithful reproduction of what you saw.

The paired browser reproduced the exact page and clarified the “org missing” confusion:

- The link resolves to “Connecting LobuSandbox.”
- The organization control is a collapsed selector, so the page initially shows only the first choice (“Atlas”).
- The authenticated claim-context actually contains all nine memberships, including “Lobu Community,” “Lobu Cloud,” “Market,” “Lobu Team,” and `buremba`.

So the org is not lost. The UX gap is that the closed selector makes this look like the only org, while the existing Enterprise install has an ownership/routing conflict that is surfaced only after a connect attempt. I’m not clicking that button because an unexpected success could move a real Slack installation. The fix should make ownership/state clear before any mutating confirmation, not rely on a dangerous probe.

The sandbox did not hang on Lobu. OpenCode’s log shows the copied OpenAI API key exhausted its billing credits, and OpenCode has been silently retrying that provider. I’m stopping the retry and switching the same visible session to the copied OpenCode OAuth provider; no session history or prompt state will be lost. This is exactly the sort of clean-sandbox gap the E2E was meant to expose.

The OAuth file is copied correctly and OpenCode recognizes “Anthropic oauth,” but this OpenCode build is not exposing any Anthropic models—only its built-in/free provider catalog. I’m checking the current official provider configuration instead of guessing a model ID. If the copied OAuth format is no longer runnable by OpenCode, I’ll use a supported free model to preserve the E2E and report that portability gap explicitly.

The fresh Lobu device login is now waiting for you:

- Email: `emrekabakci@gmail.com`
- Code: `3VZG-H2FH`
- Fallback: [approve this device](https://app.lobu.ai/oauth/device?user_code=3VZG-H2FH)

Please approve it while signed in as that exact email. OpenCode is visibly waiting in the SSH session and will not proceed until the CLI confirms authorization.

On the Slack claim-page design, I’m holding one possible enhancement because it changes the API contract and your repo rules require explicit approval first.

Proposed shape: the read-only `claim-context` response would include the exact currently owning organization (when the user is a member) and per-destination conflict status. The UI would preselect “Lobu Community,” label it as the current owner, and disable/describe unsafe Enterprise-overlap choices before any POST. No new table and no Slack credential leaves the gateway; it reads bounded connection state already stored in Postgres.

The current PR does not need this to fix the raw Slack link—it already turns it into a named link—but this enhancement would remove the misleading “Atlas is the only org / link is invalid” impression. Please tell me if you approve that contract shape; I won’t smuggle it into the existing branch without confirmation.

PR #2465 was from the earlier repair attempt, but we do not need it. I closed it because the hard-migrated canonical Slack webhook works in production; legacy aliases should remain removed.

Current findings:

- The Slack claim URL is valid and renders the LobuSandbox claim page.
- “Lobu Community” is present among all nine organizations. The collapsed selector initially displays only “Atlas,” which made it look missing.
- PR #2482 is necessary: it replaces the raw Slack URL with a named link and fixes hosted-vs-customer workspace tenancy.
- An optional claim-context enhancement could preselect the current owner and expose conflicts before submission. I need your approval for that API contract design.

Two actions are blocking completion:

1. [Approve device login](https://app.lobu.ai/oauth/device?user_code=3VZG-H2FH) as `emrekabakci@gmail.com` using code `3VZG-H2FH`.
2. Inspect the [UI comparison](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://gist.githubusercontent.com/buremba/ba38433361ce9d017220edb840f2b81d/raw/6c3ae8c14523bededf9e71c4799a5a3662e81aeb/lobu-agent-navigation-comparison.html), then post `/ui-approve 125ffeae49ca0f173a76141fd1f55f7116d63837` on [Owletto PR #714](https://github.com/lobu-ai/owletto/pull/714).

Watch the full live OpenCode session:

```sh
ssh ro-2Bw2HZT9vpyaKvxV8kuDT2Tzg@nyc1.tmate.io
```

The OpenAI key ran out of credits. The copied Anthropic OAuth was expired, so OpenCode correctly did not expose Anthropic models; I preserved the session and switched it to a working OpenCode free model. Current OpenCode guidance expects providers to be connected and selected through its provider/model flow. [OpenCode provider docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers), [model docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/models).

Reply `done` after both approvals, plus whether you approve the proposed claim-context contract.
